extracted.intended_audience: nonprofit grantseekers, development staff, executive directors seeking foundation funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for nonprofit organizations preparing and submitting grant applications to foundations, focused on avoiding common causes of rejection and improving chances of funding. Emphasizes pre-submission relationship-building, fit, compliance with funder rules, clear budgets, reporting, and realistic pipeline planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: No relationship or introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t make the mistake of submitting a grant application “cold” with no prior interaction or relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before submitting, make contact and cultivate a relationship. Identify pre-existing connections (board, staff, donor circle) who know a foundation representative to open the door; if none exist, attempt to forge one. Placing a phone call first to introduce yourself and your organization can warm up the funder to receive your proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission or program fit isn’t evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t guess at the best fit or proposal strategy—get a green light to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research the foundation’s current funding strategies; funders’ focus areas change and website info may be limited. Call or email to briefly describe your idea to ensure a good fit and check for exclusions. This contact can surface funder specifications and help you tailor your proposal to stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant application doesn’t follow directions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the foundation’s current application format, submission process, and required attachments well before the deadline so you don’t miss requirements. Follow instructions carefully and don’t cut corners—failure to follow directions can lead to immediate rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program period doesn’t match foundation’s grant cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t disregard the foundation’s funding timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the grant maker’s timeline specifications and align your project period closely with the funder’s funding period. Even worthy proposals are likely to be disqualified if the project period doesn’t match the funder’s cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget isn’t clear, correct—or even provided
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t skip a compelling financial narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a budget that follows the foundation’s required format, matches the application narrative, and shows that your funding plan is sound and achievable. Offer an accurate financial outlook that supports a clear need and sustainable strategy. Demonstrate which specific expenses the foundation’s grant would support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization didn’t meet reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t miss the chance to prove that the last grant was an investment well made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit impressive, on-time reports for previously received grants that clearly address successes and challenges and offer insights into field trends. Do not submit a new request without meeting prior reporting obligations—foundations view grants as investments and expect accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition is high, grant funding is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t let your expectations exceed your capacity or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the funding environment and research the likelihood of support (some foundations only fund 1%–10% of requests). If you are a repeat grantee with good reporting, likelihood is higher; first-time applicants face lower probability. Build a grants plan balancing mostly low-risk, higher-probability prospects with some higher-risk, lower-probability targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-decline inquiries: seek feedback and resubmission opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: When you receive a rejection, follow up to learn how to improve and whether resubmission is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrap back to the foundation for feedback and, if not yet invited, request a site visit. Two suggested brief questions: (1) 'Was our application competitive and are you willing to offer feedback on what we might improve?' and (2) 'Are you open to us resubmitting our request by the next deadline?' These inquiries can reveal helpful information to improve future applications.
